title: The HTML Boilerplate
summary: Walks line by line through the standard HTML5 boilerplate (doctype, html with lang, head with charset meta and title, body), explains nesting and indentation, and shows the VS Code ! shortcut that generates the boilerplate. Ends with a free-form 'build your own burger' exercise using invented, properly nested elements.

concepts.heading: What a boilerplate is
points: Every HTML file follows the same outer skeleton, the way a formal letter always has an address block, greeting, body and sign-off. That reusable starting skeleton is called the boilerplate.
Start every new HTML file from it, then add page content inside the body.

concepts.heading: <!DOCTYPE html>: the doctype declaration
points: Must be the very first line of the file. Its job is to declare the HTML version used, so the browser parses the document correctly.
<!DOCTYPE html> (angle bracket, exclamation mark, DOCTYPE in capitals, then html) declares HTML5, the current version.
It is a declaration, not an element: it has no closing tag.

concepts.heading: <html lang="en">: the root element
points: The html element is the root of the document. Every other element (headings, images, links, head, body) goes between <html> and </html>.
The lang attribute states the language of the text inside the element, e.g. lang="en" for English.
Sighted visitors don't notice it; screen readers and other assistive technology read it to choose the right pronunciation when reading the page aloud.
(Extra) lang also helps search engines and browser translation features, and can be set on individual elements for passages in another language.

concepts.heading: <head>: information about the page, not shown on it
points: The head holds information the browser needs to render the page correctly. Nothing in it (no text, images or links) appears in the page content area.
Two items always belong in the head: the character-set meta tag and the title.

<meta charset="UTF-8" /> sets the character encoding so every character displays correctly. Some encodings can't show emoji or symbols such as × and ÷; UTF-8 is one of the most common and covers them, so the line is normally copied in unchanged.
<title>My Website</title>: the text between the title tags is what the browser shows on the tab.
Many more tags can go in the head (the Google home page has lots of them); others will be introduced as they come up.
To inspect a real site's boilerplate in Chrome, right-click the page and choose View Page Source: doctype, html, head, charset and title are all visible near the top.

concepts.heading: <body>: all visible content
points: The body comes after the head (like a person: head, then body).
Everything the user sees goes between <body> and </body>: headings, paragraphs, images, links and every other content or structure element.
This is where almost all the work in the HTML sections of the course happens.

concepts.heading: Nesting and indentation
points: Elements sit inside other elements: head and body inside html, h1 and img inside body. This is nesting, and it becomes increasingly important throughout the course.
The analogy used is a burger: html is the top and bottom bun, body is a pair of tomato slices inside it, and the page content is sandwiched between those.
A short element whose opening and closing tags fit easily on one line (e.g. <title>My Website</title>) can stay on one line; it still has a start and an end.

Indent each nested level (two spaces in the slides) so every closing tag lines up vertically with its opening tag. Correct indentation shows at a glance which element contains which and keeps code tidy.
When starting out, type the boilerplate by hand a few times to learn it before relying on the shortcut.

concepts.heading: VS Code shortcut: ! then Enter
points: In a file saved with the .html extension, type ! and press Enter on the first suggestion; VS Code (via its built-in Emmet) inserts the whole boilerplate.
It only works once the file has been named/saved as something.html; with any other extension the suggestion does not appear.
The generated version contains two extra meta tags not covered above.
<meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge"> exists only for Internet Explorer compatibility. IE is retired, so this line can be deleted to keep the file clean.
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> controls how the page is sized relative to the screen it opens on, i.e. how the browser displays it initially.

(Extra) width=device-width makes the layout width match the device's screen width instead of a phone pretending to be ~980px wide, and initial-scale=1.0 means no zoom on load. This matters a lot once responsive CSS is introduced. Recent Emmet versions already leave out the X-UA-Compatible line.
The default <title>Document</title> should be replaced with a real page title.

concepts.heading: Attributes refresher
points: An attribute goes inside the opening tag as name="value" (name, equals sign, value in quotes).
An element can carry as many attributes as needed, separated by spaces.

code_examples.caption: Minimal HTML5 boilerplate, annotated
code_examples.code: Hello World

code_examples.caption: What VS Code's ! + Enter generates (Emmet); the X-UA-Compatible line can be deleted
code_examples.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    
</body>
</html>

code_examples.caption: Build-your-own-burger exercise: invented elements practising nesting, attributes and indentation (illustrative)
code_examples.code:
<bun type="brioche" toasted="yes">
  <sauce flavour="chipotle"></sauce>
  <lettuce leaves="2"></lettuce>
  <patty kind="bean" cooked="well-done">
    <cheese style="smoked"></cheese>
  </patty>
  <tomato slices="3"></tomato>
  <pickles></pickles>
</bun>

task.name: Build your own burger (nesting practice)
task.starting_point: No starter files. Open VS Code and create any new .html file (or practise in the same file where you typed out the boilerplate).
task.goal: Describe an imaginary burger as HTML-style code using invented elements, to practise opening/closing tags, attributes and nesting with clean indentation.
steps: First, type the full boilerplate from memory in a new .html file, then try the ! + Enter shortcut and compare the two.
Create an outer bun element with an opening and closing tag, and give it one or more attributes in name="value" form.
Inside the bun, add whatever fillings you like as their own elements (tomato, lettuce, patty, cheese, sauce...), each with opening and closing tags.
Nest at least one element inside another filling to create a deeper level.
Indent each nested level so every closing tag lines up with its opening tag.
Optionally share your burger code in the course Q&A.
task.expected_result: A neatly indented block where it is obvious which elements sit inside which, and every opening tag has a matching closing tag. (Invented tags won't render as anything meaningful; the point is the structure.)

pitfalls: Putting visible content (headings, images, paragraphs) inside head instead of body.
Typing ! in a file that hasn't been saved with a .html extension and wondering why no boilerplate appears.
Poor indentation that hides which element a closing tag belongs to; mismatched or missing closing tags in nested code.
Treating <!DOCTYPE html> as an element and trying to close it, or placing anything above it.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet. Every s04 lesson's starter code already includes a doctype, html lang, head with charset and title, and body, but nothing explains those lines. The viewport meta tag is only explained later, in s08.
gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 's04-boilerplate' (place it between 4.2 Multi-Page Websites and 4.3 Portfolio). Blurb: every HTML file shares one skeleton; learn what each line does, then let the editor write it for you.

Tasks: (1) start from an empty file and type the boilerplate from memory; (2) set the title so the tab text changes; (3) set lang to a language other than English and add a paragraph in that language; (4) move an h1 into the head and observe that browsers silently relocate it, then put it back in the body; (5) build an indented 'burger' of invented nested elements with attributes.

Starter code idea: a file containing only

Hello

, with a checker that confirms doctype first, html lang present, head with meta charset and title, body containing the h1.

Explore demo: a clickable, colour-coded boilerplate where hovering each line highlights its nesting level (burger layers) and shows a one-sentence explanation; a toggle shows the Emmet ! output with the X-UA-Compatible line struck through as obsolete.
Explore demo 2: a charset switcher that renders the same text with emoji and × ÷ symbols decoded as UTF-8 vs ISO-8859-1, showing the garbled output when the encoding is wrong.
Notes: add the 'View Page Source' tip and the rule that ! only works in files saved as .html.
